content.title: About
content.content: Rosemary (Salvia rosmarinus) is an evergreen aromatic shrub in the mint family, native to the Mediterranean. It has tough needle-like leaves with a pine-like, camphor-spicy aroma and a slightly bitter flavor. Rosemary is used fresh and dried for meat, potatoes, bread, marinades, oils, and sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name rosemary comes from Latin words meaning sea dew.
In 2017, botanists moved rosemary into the sage genus and began calling it Salvia rosmarinus.
In ancient times, rosemary was considered a symbol of remembrance and fidelity.
It pairs excellently with grilled meat, potatoes, and bread, such as focaccia.
Tough rosemary sprigs can be used in place of skewers.

items.title: Contains essential oils
items.content: Aromatic compounds give rosemary its characteristic smell.

items.title: Adds flavor without calories or salt
items.content: Fragrant herbs make dishes more flavorful without extra salt or fat.

items.title: May reduce harmful compounds when grilling
items.content: A marinade with rosemary may reduce the formation of harmful compounds when grilling meat.

items.title: Contains a small amount of minerals
items.content: The herb contains calcium, iron, and manganese, but the amounts in a dish are small.

items.title: Large amounts and pregnancy
items.content: Rosemary is safe in food amounts, but large amounts and concentrated supplements during pregnancy should be discussed with a doctor.

items.title: Epilepsy and essential oil
items.content: Rosemary essential oil contains camphor and may trigger seizures; it should not be taken internally, and people with epilepsy should be careful.

items.title: Medications
items.content: In large amounts, rosemary may affect how anticoagulants and some other medications work.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Allergic reactions and contact dermatitis are possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Finely chop the rosemary needles and add them to meat, chicken, fish, potatoes, vegetables, bread, soups, marinades, and oils. Fresh sprigs can be put whole into a dish and removed before serving. Less dried rosemary is needed than fresh.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh sprigs in the refrigerator, wrapped in a damp paper towel, for one to two weeks, or freeze or dry them. Keep dried rosemary in an airtight jar in a dry, dark place.
